Thank you Mr. President. This bill focuses on three core goals, balancing screen time with teacher-led instruction, creating consistent statewide expectations for school technology policies, and introducing responsible and thoughtful AI integration in education.

It preserves local control. The state board provides a model policy, but each LEA adopts and may amend the policy to fit local needs. And it must be adopted through a public meeting with opportunity for come.

This is not a one size fits all approach. The bill establishes clear expectations for instructional technology before it is used in classrooms. LEAs must ensure the technology has significant educational value supports instruction is free from distracting features is safe for students, cognitive and emotional development and supports teachers rather than replacing direct

instruction, it addresses the growing concern about non-essential screen time. LEAs must minimize screen time that is not instructional prior. Prioritize purposeful use and ensure that technology enhances learning outcomes.

The principle is simple. Technology should be a tool for learning, not a replacement for teaching. Excuse me. The bill also introduces a developmentally appropriate framework for technology use across grade levels.

In grades K through 12, there are no take home devices, no required one-on-one device ratios and screen use is limited to basic computer science introduction and required testing in grades four through six. Technology use is limited and supervised in middle school devices are primarily used on campus with opt-in policies for take home use in high school, take home devices are allowed

unless parents choose to opt out. The bill recognizes that some students struggle with tech-based learning. So it also requires LEAs to create resource plans to support students who experience technology related learning difficulties.

It also responsibly prepares students for the future by adding AI literacy to the core computer science standards. While establishing guardrails, teachers retain professional judgment. AI cannot be used as the sole grading authority.
AI cannot make high stake student decisions and parents must be notified when AI tools are used in instruction. Importantly, this bill is not anti-technology. It does not ban computers.
It does not remove local flexibility and does not restrict online schools or IEP accommodations. It simply ensures technology is used thoughtfully and responsibly.
In summary, Mr. President HB 2 73 second sub as amended brings balance to technology use in classrooms by setting statewide guardrails while preserving local control.

It prioritizes student development.
